headline: Wall Street ends at the day's lows as the AI sell-off spreads to banks and miners
tone: The day finished risk-off: what began as a chip shakeout in Asia became a broad de-risking by the US close, with no buyers stepping in ahead of Nvidia's results.
body: Nvidia lost 4.1% after CNBC reported the board is not discussing bringing Jensen Huang back, and the Commerce Department closed the loophole that let Chinese firms rent Nvidia computing power in third countries such as Singapore. The Philadelphia chip index fell 5.3% with all 30 members down; Micron and Intel lost about 7% each.

The selling broadened in the afternoon. Banks that finance the AI data-centre build-out fell too, with Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs down about 3% each, and copper, gold and uranium miners were sold with them. That points to crowded positions being cut across the whole AI-capex chain, not a view on one company.

There was no flight to safety in bonds: Treasury yields held up and the dollar firmed, so investors raised cash rather than buying duration. Fed Chair Warsh gave no rate guidance; his three AI scenarios included one where AI returns disappoint and stocks fall, which did nothing to calm the market.

Oil fell even though Iran's Revolutionary Guards said two more tankers hit mines in Hormuz. The IEA's fourth-quarter surplus call and reports that the US is not planning imminent strikes on Iran outweighed the attacks. European gas also fell hard on mild weather forecasts and record US LNG exports.

views.text: Priced in for Tuesday: more caution into Nvidia's results on Tuesday night. What would turn it: a clear CEO succession plan or guidance showing demand from China and overseas data centres survives the new export rules. A weak guide would test the banks and miners next, not just the chip names.

The market is trading the surplus, not the war: Brent settled near the day's low despite the mine strikes. Only lost loadings at Gulf terminals or a halt to Hormuz traffic would bring the risk premium back.
